newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries remain tightly range bound at midday.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries remain tightly range bound at midday.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices remained tightly range bound at midday on Monday as economic data releases failed to shake the market out of its torpor.
Trading volume remained thin as investors apparently have mostly closed their books on 1996 and were anticipating an early close on Tuesday.

The release of slightly stronger-than-expected existing home sales -- up 1.8 percent to annualized rate of 4.04 million in November -- and leading economic indicators had little impact on the market Monday morning.
Helping to underpin the market was the strong U.S. dollar, which remained firm in overnight trading in Europe and Tokyo. The dollar had risen to a 45-month high against the Japanese yen on Friday.
The short end enjoyed early support before losing ground to the 30-year in later trade. Many investors seeking dollar-denominated assets like the liquidity and safety of the short end.
The three-month bill was up five basis points at 5.02 percent. The 30-year bond also has gained 8/32 at 99-24/32 to yield 6.52 percent.

"Imagine what would have happened if there was anybody around to react to this information," he asked.
However, for now most trading desks remain half-staffed and activity is very thin, Zukowsky said.

Donald Straszheim, chief economist at Merrill Lynch & Co., predicted bonds would remain in their recent trading ranges as long as economic data continue to paint a mixed picture. The Federal Reserve likely will remain on hold and keep its target for the federal funds rate at 5.25 percent during the next meeting of the policy-making Federal Open Market Committee on Feb. 4 and 5, he said.

Straszheim noted that the dollar should continue to strengthen and would probably surpass the 120 yen level before the end of 1997. The U.S., he said, enjoyed a 300 to 400 basis point interest rate advantage over Japan.
In light trade, 10-year notes were up 1/32 to 101-17/32, yielding 6.29 percent.
Five-year notes were up 1/32 to 100-6/32, yielding 6.08 percent. Two-year notes were up 1/32 to 99-30/32, yielding 5.78 percent.
Six-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.07 percent. Year bill rates were unchanged 5.18 percent.
